name: c3-watchdog
description: The c3-watchdog panel as an Android app: a WebView showing the REAL dashboard, drawn by c3-watchdog-tui inside nix-on-droid and transcribed to HTML.

build.external_inputs_doc: Artifacts this APK bakes in from ANOTHER repo, so the publish gate can see them. The gate hashes git objects and none of these are in this repo: the panel binary was rebuilt with fixes, this app's own source had not moved, and the gate skipped publishing forever while every rebuild agreed the APK was current.

_doc: The app owns no layout. It asks the terminal for a screen at the grid this device actually has and injects what comes back. Every previous attempt to re-draw that dashboard outside the panel diverged on frames, alignment and colour, so nothing here reproduces any of it.

watchdog._doc: Baked into libs:watchdog as WATCHDOG_TARGETS_JSON_B64 / _CMD. Host, port, user and the command are DATA, never Kotlin constants — the same rule cloud-ide's terminal-targets.json follows. Loopback because Android shares 127.0.0.1 across app sandboxes. Auth is key-based and the key is generated in-app: add the public line (Setup screen) to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys in the env. The app pushes its own panel and sampler into the env's cache at connect time and runs them from there, so a bare nix-on-droid needs nothing installed — only the ssh key, which the env's own installer provisions.

nix-on-droid.label: Nix-on-Droid
nix-on-droid._doc: 8024, read off the device, not the 8022 that was assumed: nix-on-droid's sshd_config sets Port 8024 on this phone. Data, so a phone that differs is a one-line change here.

tools._doc: Where libs:watchdog fetches the binaries it SHIPS. The APK carries them; nothing is ever installed on the phone. aarch64 static musl, because that is every Android device this decade and musl does not care which libc the environment has — or whether it has one.

modules._doc: settings.gradle iterates this (FIRE rule 6: never hardcode the list). `dir` is how a module is SHARED by reference rather than copied: the lib lives once in ab_cloud-libs-shared/libs and every app points at that one directory, so a fix lands in all of them at build time.

toolchain._doc: Pinned for reproducibility — all derived in flake.nix. Mirrors aa_cloud-superapp / ea_cloud-comms pins so all the Android projects share one toolchain story. Node is added for the Acode (Cordova) fork's JS/plugin build.

signing._doc: ONE shared Cloud-constellation signing key for ALL Android apps (Cloud-Comms hub+forks, Cloud-Nav, Cloud-IDE, Cloud-SuperApp). The SAME key signs every app so cross-app signature-IPC + the in-app fleet updater never hit a signature mismatch. KEY LOCATION (raw credential + sops passwords live ONLY in the vault repo): A0_keys/providers/android/release.jks (OU=Cloud Constellation) + A0_keys/providers/android/signing.secrets.yaml. build.sh::_resolve_signing resolves $VAULT_DIR (default ~/git/cloud-vault) + sops-decrypts the passwords, exporting ANDROID_KEYSTORE_FILE/ANDROID_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD/ANDROID_KEY_ALIAS/ANDROID_KEY_PASSWORD which the gradle signingConfig reads. CI does the same via a vault checkout + the SOPS_AGE_KEY secret. THERE IS NO FALLBACK: if the key is unavailable the build FAILS LOUD telling you to use the one shared key — it never generates or substitutes a random/legacy key.
signing._doc_ssh: The ONE declared ssh key every constellation app uses to reach a phone terminal, resolved exactly like the ONE signing key: from the vault, sops-decrypted by build.sh::_resolve_ssh_key, baked to BuildConfig.CLOUD_SSH_KEY_B64, never hardcoded and never generated. The public half is committed in the open at cloud-u-linux/da__my-konsole/termux/authorized_keys, which is what the env provisions — so a phone trusts the key before any app is installed and there is no paste-this-line setup step. NO FALLBACK: a build without the vault fails rather than shipping an app that mints a key the phone has never heard of.

release._doc: Per-APK distribution, the same data-driven block every app here has. build.sh oras-push + gh-release read it; the workflow only invokes those engine commands and hardcodes no registry or tag. This block is ALSO what makes the app discoverable: aa_cloud-superapp/data/regen.sh admits a sibling on .android.application_id + .release.ghcr, so registering in the constellation is a property of the app rather than a list to edit. {sha} -> git short sha, {version_name} -> android.version_name.

ghcr._doc: ENABLED. It was disabled when packages came out private — the cause was the login preferring secrets.GHCR_TOKEN, a PAT, which creates an ACCOUNT-owned package that is born private and cannot be patched. Every workflow here logs in with GITHUB_TOKEN now, which creates the package FOR THE REPOSITORY and takes the repository's visibility; verified on cloud-u-linux, whose first GITHUB_TOKEN push produced a public package. The workflow checks after every push and says so if it ever regresses.

auto_update._doc: The in-app updater reads release_url first (libs:updater Fleet.kt) and only falls back to GHCR, which this app no longer publishes — so updates come off the release asset, which follows repo visibility. NOTE: version_code is 1 and never bumped, so this channel is inert until it is.

gh_release._doc: rolling_tag is canonical: one release the ship workflow overwrites on every main push, so /releases/latest/download/C3-Watchdog.apk is a stable URL.

variants._doc: The same shape ac_cloud-browser and every other per-ABI app declares. Without it both matrix legs uploaded ONE asset name to the rolling release and raced: the second leg's --clobber deleted the first's asset mid-upload, which surfaced as HTTP 404 on the assets endpoint. Worse than the error, the winner was arbitrary — an x86_64 APK could land as C3-Watchdog.apk and be installed on an arm64 phone.
